# The tear-out opt-ins ride an overridable hook and vanish silently

## Context

Measured on a consumer whose multi-window dock looked finished and had two entire gestures dead.

`Workspace#getDockProjectionOptions` is the base hook that arms tear-out:

```js
getDockProjectionOptions() {
    return this.enableDockTearOutLifecycle
        ? {enableDockTearOut: true, ...this.tearOutHandlers}
        : {}
}
```

It is also the natural hook for a host to override — it is the documented way to thread projection options. A host that overrides it and returns its own object, without spreading `super`, discards `enableDockTearOut` and the whole handler bundle.

**Nothing reports it.** The projection succeeds, the dock renders, and the pop-out action still appears — so the host's own acceptance signal says multi-window works.

Live latest-open sweep: latest 20 open issues at 2026-09-03T11:16:37Z; no equivalent. A2A claim sweep: no competing claim.

## The Problem

Two gestures die, and the third keeps working in a way that hides them.

- **Dragging a tab out of the dock becomes unreachable.** `enableDockTearOut` is what sets `allowOverdrag` and `enableProxyToPopup` on every tab sort zone (`projection/LayoutAdapter.mjs:1253-1255`). Without it the proxy stays clamped to its tab strip, and the adapter's own comment states the consequence exactly: *"the boundary-exit grammar reads the LIVE proxy rect, and while the proxy is clamped to the tab-strip boundary the intersection ratio never drops — the exit cannot fire."* The user cannot drag past the boundary at all; it does not read as disabled, it reads as broken.
- **A dragged popup finds no target.** `crossWindowSortGroup` becomes `sortGroup` on the zone (`:1256`), and `manager.DragCoordinator` keys its registry by sort group — `sortZones.get(sortGroup)?.get(windowId)`. A null group means the zone never registers, so a popup dragged over the window highlights no drop areas.
- **The pop-out ACTION still renders**, because `dockPopOutActionActive` derives from `tearOutHandlers` **on the instance**, not from the projection context. So the one path that does not read the context keeps working, and it is the path a host is most likely to test first.

That last point is what makes this worth a ticket rather than a consumer footnote: the failure is not just silent, it is **masked by a working sibling**. A host can pop a pane out, close it, watch it come home, and reasonably conclude the feature is delivered.

This is the #18151 class with an extra turn of the screw — the engine does not merely ask a host to re-derive what it knows, it hands the host a way to drop it and then reports success.

## The Architectural Reality

- `src/dashboard/dock/Workspace.mjs` — `getDockProjectionOptions()` is the sole carrier of `enableDockTearOut` and `tearOutHandlers` into the context.
- `src/dashboard/dock/projection/LayoutAdapter.mjs:1253-1256` — where the three zone flags are derived from it.
- `Workspace#dockPopOutActionActive` — derived from the instance bundle, which is why the action survives the loss.
- The same method's JSDoc already documents that **two** related inconsistencies *"throw at projection rather than silently unaddressing an action"*. The mechanism this ticket needs is therefore already precedented in the very method that loses the options.

## The Fix

Preferred: **throw at projection** when `enableDockTearOutLifecycle` is `true` but the resolved projection context carries no `enableDockTearOut`. Same shape, same place, same rationale as the two violations already guarded there — a host that meant to enable tear-out learns immediately, and a host that meant to disable it turns the lifecycle flag off rather than dropping the options.

Alternative, if the throw is judged too strict: apply the base wiring **outside** the overridable hook, so the host's override composes with it rather than replacing it. Cleaner in that a host cannot get it wrong, but it makes the hook's return value no longer the whole context, which is a bigger contract change than the guard.

Either way the host-facing rule wants stating in the hook's JSDoc: an override must spread `super`.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] AC-1 — a workspace with `enableDockTearOutLifecycle: true` whose `getDockProjectionOptions` override omits `super` fails loudly at projection, naming the dropped option.
- [ ] AC-2 — a workspace with the lifecycle **off** and no `enableDockTearOut` projects silently, as today; the guard must not fire on a host that never wanted tear-out.
- [ ] AC-3 — a workspace whose override spreads `super` projects unchanged, with `allowOverdrag`, `enableProxyToPopup` and `sortGroup` all reaching the zone.
- [ ] AC-4 — red-first: the arm fails on current source, where the omission projects successfully.
- [ ] AC-5 — the hook's JSDoc states that an override must spread `super`, and why the pop-out action cannot be used as evidence that it did.
- [ ] AC-6 — the existing tear-out and pop-out suites stay green.

## Out of Scope

- `crossWindowSortGroup` having no engine default. A sort group is a deployment-wide name a host must choose, so requiring it is correct; this ticket is about the options the engine *does* own being droppable.
- The vessel conversion thresholds.
- Whether `dockPopOutActionActive` should derive from the context instead of the instance — arguably it should, so the action tracks the same truth as the gestures, but that is a separate design question and changing it would alter when the action hides.

## Avoided Traps

- **Documenting it and calling it done.** The reason this survived in a consumer for a full session is not absent documentation, it is that the pop-out action kept working and supplied a false pass. A doc line does not reach someone who already believes the feature is delivered.
- **Treating it as consumer error.** It is, locally — the override should have spread `super`. But an engine that routes its own load-bearing wiring through a host-overridable hook, and then reports success when the host replaces it, has handed out the footgun. The guard is the engine's to add.
- **Guarding on the handler bundle instead of the context.** Checking `tearOutHandlers` would pass in exactly the broken case: the bundle is on the instance and intact. The context is the thing that must be inspected.

## Decision Record impact

`none` — a projection-time guard consistent with two existing ones in the same method.
